description: Tang Yuan are soft, chewy glutinous rice balls often served in a sweet ginger soup. They symbolize togetherness and are a traditional delicacy enjoyed during Chinese festivals. This delightful dessert offers a comforting blend of textures and flavors, perfect for any occasion.

instructions.title: Prepare the Filling
instructions.text: Toast black sesame seeds lightly until fragrant. Grind them into a fine powder. Mix with granulated sugar and melted lard or vegetable oil until a paste forms. Refrigerate for 15 minutes to firm up, then roll into small balls, about 5g each.

instructions.title: Make the Dough
instructions.text: In a large bowl, gradually add warm water to the glutinous rice flour, mixing until a soft, pliable dough forms. Knead for about 5 minutes until smooth. The dough should not be too sticky or too dry.

instructions.title: Form the Tang Yuan
instructions.text: Pinch off small pieces of dough, about 15g each. Flatten each piece into a disk. Place one sesame filling ball in the center, then carefully gather the dough around the filling and roll gently between your palms to form a smooth ball.

instructions.title: Prepare the Ginger Soup
instructions.text: In a medium pot, combine 1 liter of water, sliced ginger, and rock sugar. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 15-20 minutes to allow the ginger flavor to infuse.

instructions.title: Cook the Tang Yuan
instructions.text: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Carefully drop the formed Tang Yuan into the boiling water. Stir gently to prevent sticking.

instructions.title: Serve
instructions.text: Once the Tang Yuan float to the surface and swell slightly, about 3-5 minutes, they are cooked. Ladle the cooked Tang Yuan into bowls with the hot ginger soup. Serve immediately.

tips: For perfectly smooth Tang Yuan, ensure your dough is well-kneaded and has the right consistency, not too dry or too wet. Adjust water or flour slightly if needed.
If you dont have black sesame seeds, you can use crushed peanuts or red bean paste for alternative fillings, offering different traditional flavors.
Tang Yuan are best enjoyed fresh and warm. If you have leftovers, store them in the soup in the refrigerator and reheat gently, though the texture might be slightly softer.
